title: The discovery of penicillin
subtitle: Fleming, 1928
subject: sciences
description: In 1928, Alexander Fleming noticed that a mold had killed bacteria on a culture dish. From this chance the first great antibiotic was born.

hero.hook: A forgotten box, a mold, and the medicine turns upside down.

blocks.text: Before antibiotics, a simple infection could kill. A cut, pneumonia, a war wound: the body often fought alone.

In **1928**, the Scottish doctor **Alexander Fleming** accidentally discovered a substance capable of killing bacteria. It will be called **penicillin**. But it will still take years to make it into a real medicine.
Fleming studies bacteria in London. Coming back from vacation, he looks at old culture boxes. On one of them, a **mold** grew. Around her, the bacteria are dead.

blocks.caption: Fleming and the key idea: something in the mold stops the bacteria.

blocks.text: The mold belongs to the genus **Penicillium**. Fleming understands that it produces an antibacterial substance. He calls it penicillin. But he cannot purify it enough to treat the sick.
Fleming later said that if he had been more orderly, he would have thrown the box away. The mess in the lab helped the discovery.

At the beginning of the **1940** years, in Oxford, **Howard Florey** and **Ernst Chain** returned to work. With their team, they isolated, concentrated and tested penicillin on animals, then on humans.
The Second World War made things urgent: infected soldiers had to be treated. Penicillin moves from the laboratory to a strategic issue.

blocks.caption: It was necessary to invent industrial ways of growing mold.

blocks.text: To treat millions of people, enormous quantities are needed. The United States industrialized production during the war. Giant vats make mold miss like beer.
In **1945**, Fleming, Florey and Chain received the Nobel Prize. Medicine is entering the age of antibiotics.
Today, too many misused antibiotics have allowed certain bacteria to become **resistant**: the drugs no longer kill them. Fleming had already warned of this risk.

Penicillin was born from a coincidence observed by Fleming in **1928**, then became a medicine thanks to Florey, Chain and the war industry. It has saved millions of lives... as long as you don't wear it out.
